Michelangelo Buonarroti. The Italian Renaissance master of sculpture, painting, and architecture whose works define the High Renaissance ideal. His monumental marble and fresco figures—from the David to the Pietà to the Sistine Chapel ceiling—combine anatomical precision with spiritual intensity, embodying the Renaissance fusion of humanism and divine aspiration. Working across three art forms and across nearly nine decades, Michelangelo established a standard of artistic genius and technical perfection that has remained unmatched. He was simultaneously a revolutionary who transformed what art could be and a traditionalist who perfected inherited forms.

Michelangelo carved the David in 1504, a seventeen-foot marble nude that became the symbol of Renaissance Florence, human potential, and idealized masculine beauty—a figure of serene power carved from a block other sculptors had abandoned. He sculpted the Pietà from 1498 to 1499, a marble group of Mary cradling the dead Christ that perfected Renaissance pathos and technical delicacy. The drapery, the facial expressions, the geometry of grief—all rendered in flawless marble. Michelangelo created the Moses in 1515 for the tomb of Pope Julius the Second, a bearded figure whose intensity and barely-contained power suggest divine knowledge barely constrained in human form. He produced the Rondanini Pietà, unfinished, in 1564, carved in his eighties, proving his artistic vision remained vital decades after the celebrated earlier works.

Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling from 1508 to 1512, a vast fresco of biblical scenes spanning creation, fall, and redemption, including the iconic Creation of Adam—one of Western art's most reproduced images, a visual theology of human dignity. He created frescoes of such scale and complexity that he essentially invented the grand-scale monumental fresco as a Renaissance form. The ceiling required him to work on scaffolding while lying on his back. The Last Judgment from 1536 to 1541 on the Sistine Chapel's altar wall depicts the resurrection and divine judgment with anatomical precision and apocalyptic drama—a later, more austere and troubled work than the ceiling.

Michelangelo designed the dome of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, the Renaissance's architectural apex, a structure combining geometric perfection with structural innovation. He was known for his terribilità—a style of overwhelming, almost violent grandeur and realism, a departure from earlier Renaissance sweetness toward intensity and psychological power. As an artist-theorist, Michelangelo treated sculpture as the supreme art form, believing the artist liberates the figure imprisoned in the stone—a philosophical claim that elevated sculptural practice.

Michelangelo achieved in his lifetime something almost no artist does: he was recognized as a genius by his contemporaries and remains uncontroversially considered one of history's greatest artists five centuries later. His works established or codified High Renaissance aesthetics—the heroic nude male figure, the integration of architecture and sculpture, the monumental scale of fresco, the fusion of anatomy and spirituality. His influence on subsequent art is incalculable. Every neoclassical sculptor studied him, every academic painter learned from his figure drawing, and contemporary artists still wrestle with his shadow. The paradox of Michelangelo is that his technical perfection and his expressive power are inseparable: his genius for anatomy, his mastery of marble, his command of fresco technique all serve an artistic vision of profound spiritual and humanistic depth. The Sistine Chapel ceiling remains perhaps the single most consequential artwork in Western visual culture, a ceiling that has reshaped how billions of people imagine creation, judgment, and the human condition. He shared a father with Leonardo da Vinci, that contemporary rival and fellow Renaissance polymath, and the two artists embodied different approaches to genius. Raphael completed the trinity of High Renaissance masters. Yet it is Michelangelo who remains the measure by which artistic greatness is judged.
